GPS finds you by timing signals from satellites 20,000 km overhead.
Relativity makes those clocks drift 38 microseconds a day — that's 11.4 km of position error.

youtube.title: Your Phone Uses Einstein's Relativity Every Day
youtube.description:
Without Einstein, your GPS drifts 10 km every day.

GPS satellites orbit 20,000 km up and time their signals at the speed of light.
Special relativity slows their clocks by 7 microseconds a day; general relativity adds 45 back.
The net drift is 38 microseconds — which multiplies out to 11.4 km of position error.

So engineers built each clock to tick slow on the ground, so it arrives right in orbit.

Save this one.

Formula lines build the relativistic correction step by step: −7 μs/day from special relativity, +45 μs/day from general relativity, net +38 μs/day, then multiplied by the speed of light to give 11.4 km/day of position error.
